body.text: Before Xi Jinping rose to power in 2012, China’s global strategy was one of biding its time and hiding its strength. The concept was coined by supreme leader Deng Xiaoping in 1989 in the wake of the Tiananmen protests and remained largely unchanged under his successors Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao.

But once Xi came to power, China’s outward-looking foreign policy took off. In 2013, Xi travelled widely and launched the Belt and Road Initiative, which has become the world’s largest source of bilateral finance. And in the years that followed, China spearheaded many international initiatives and took a lead role in addressing global issues.

At the same time, China rapidly built up its navy and network of bases in the South China Sea and staffed its embassies with increasingly assertive diplomats. The pace has been so fast that many have been left wondering what China really wants.

In China’s Global Strategy under Xi Jinping, Steve Tsang and Olivia Cheung attempt to answer this question, analyse Xi’s global thinking, and provide pointers about what we can expect in coming years.

Tsang is the director of the China Institute at SOAS University of London and Cheung is a lecturer at King’s College London. Both have published widely on Chinese politics, including a 2024 analysis of Xi Jinping’s political thought.

While taking a realistic view of China’s foreign policy, the authors reject straightforward neoclassical realism as inadequate. China has much in common with other great-power hegemons, but its political system and leadership arrangements are also in many ways unique. To account for this difference, the authors have developed a tailor-made approach that they call ‘Sinocentric party-state realism’.

The foundation for China’s foreign policy is provided by Xi Jinping Thought, which was enshrined in the constitution in 2018 and has assumed the status of an official ideology. Its proclaimed aim is to fulfil ‘the China dream of national rejuvenation’ and transform China into a ‘modern socialist country’ by 2050.

China wants to be an international rule-maker rather than a rule-taker. It views the current international order as Western-led and would like to democratise international relations by replacing it with a Sinocentric order aligned with the interests of most of the world’s countries – that is, the Global South.

To achieve this, China is using its entire foreign-policy toolkit. While the current US administration has shunned multilateralism, China is making full use of the United Nations, international financial institutions and south–south cooperation mechanisms, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the BRICS meetings.

As the authors see it, China is not seeking to take over the US’s role as global policeman, but rather to transform the world order into something different. They refer extensively to tianxia (‘all under heaven’) and Pax Sinica, terms that describe the relative stability that prevailed in East Asia and parts of Central Asia under the tributary system of successive Chinese dynasties.

Overriding the other foreign policy drivers is the priority of keeping Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party in power. However, the personalised nature of Xi’s foreign policy also carries risks. With less than a year to go until the next CCP National Congress, Xi has shown no signs of designating a successor and has been careful to keep potential competitors out of the party’s leadership. The authors remind us that personalised ideologies seldom endure.

What can we expect from the future? The authors predict that China will seek to upend the current order in two stages. First, making use of the US’s withdrawal from international leadership, China will mobilise the support of the Global South to transform the world order. Second, by 2050 China will take control of Taiwan, preferably by peaceful means, in the process exposing the ineffectiveness of US security guarantees.
Tsang concludes with a postscript for Western policymakers. His recommendations focus on two pivots: the crucial role assigned to the Global South, and the Taiwan question.

To dissuade the Global South from aligning with China, the West needs to broaden the appeal of the current world order, in Tsang’s view. This would require a realignment of decision-making in international institutions and a massive injection of beneficiary-friendly development finance. And the West would need a comprehensive plan to pre-empt a Chinese takeover of Taiwan. Neither issue has recently received much attention.

China’s Global Strategy under Xi Jinping is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand China’s global ambitions. Tsang and Cheung have immersed themselves in their topic, reviewing a wide range of source materials. As a result, their book sheds important new light on Xi’s foreign policy doctrine. It also includes a fascinating chapter on the institutions that formulate China’s foreign policy.

However, the book’s strength is also a weakness. The authors are so steeped in Xi Jinping speak that at times the line between analysing China’s policies and accepting them at face value becomes blurred, with critical review taking a back seat.
